questions.prompt: What defines a transaction in this lecture's read/write model?
options: A sequence of operations that performs one logical task
Exactly one SELECT statement
Exactly one disk-page write
Every operation from DBMS startup to shutdown
questions.explanation: One logical task can involve several statements. A transaction is not the same as one SELECT statement or one I/O operation.

questions.prompt: T moves 3 items from warehouse A to B. After subtracting from A, T requests ROLLBACK. What should happen?
options: Only the subtraction from A is retained
Both A and B return to their values before T
The system automatically adds to B and commits
Every change already in RAM is retained
questions.explanation: Aborting must remove the effects of the entire transaction. Having written a change to RAM does not justify retaining it.

questions.prompt: How does the DBMS primarily represent a transaction's computation?
options: Every computation on a local variable is a database write
Only final changes matter, so all reads are ignored
As reads and writes of data objects
Only SQL updates count; SELECT statements are ignored
questions.explanation: The abstraction represents database reads and writes. Local computation and real-world side effects do not automatically become recoverable database operations.

questions.prompt: Why can interleaving improve throughput while a transaction waits for disk I/O?
options: Each disk read becomes physically faster
It eliminates all data conflicts
It reduces the number of instructions in every transaction
The CPU can work on another transaction
questions.explanation: Interleaving makes use of time spent waiting for resources. It does not change the physical speed of I/O or guarantee that conflicts disappear.

questions.prompt: T has sent an email, and its database transaction then rolls back. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Rolling back the database does not automatically recall the email
The email is always recalled together with the data changes
COMMIT is automatically executed to retain the email
Every DBMS records emails in its WAL
questions.explanation: Sending an email is outside the database read/write model presented here. Database atomicity does not automatically extend to external email delivery.

questions.prompt: After crash recovery completes, a transfer's debit remains but its corresponding credit is missing. Which property is directly violated?
options: Durability, because the transaction definitely committed
Atomicity
Isolation between concurrent transactions
Consistency only at the level of a NOT NULL constraint
questions.explanation: Retaining only part of a transaction's effects violates atomicity. Without knowing that the transaction committed, we cannot attribute the problem solely to durability.

questions.prompt: An application commits a transfer that incorrectly increases total stock by 2 units, even without concurrency. Who is primarily responsible for the logical error?
options: Isolation automatically repairs the incorrect formula
Atomicity infers every undeclared invariant
The application must implement transactions that preserve the invariant
COMMIT guarantees that every business rule has been checked automatically
questions.explanation: Transaction consistency depends on the application's logic. Isolation cannot repair a transaction that is already incorrect when run alone.

questions.prompt: The user sees a successful COMMIT, but a crash loses an update that the system promised to preserve. Which property is violated?
options: Isolation, because the read/write order changed
Atomicity, simply because the transaction contained several writes
Consistency, simply because a CHECK constraint was declared
Durability
questions.explanation: Durability protects committed effects. Isolation concerns concurrent interactions rather than whether data survives a crash.

questions.prompt: Two transactions are correct when run separately, but their interleaving reports an incorrect total. Which property requires concurrency control?
options: Isolation
Durability, achieved by flushing every read
Atomicity without any control of interleaving
Only a separate CHECK constraint on each column
questions.explanation: Isolation controls interleaving so transactions do not observe inappropriate intermediate states. Atomicity and log flushing alone do not determine a safe concurrent access order.

questions.prompt: How does logging support atomicity in the introductory explanation?
options: It prevents every transaction from ever aborting
It retains enough information to undo an aborted transaction's effects
It stores only COMMIT records, with no update information
It replays aborted transactions' effects without undoing them
questions.explanation: The log provides information for reversing changes. Atomicity does not mean that transactions can never fail.

questions.prompt: Where does a transaction make its changes under the lecture's shadow-paging approach?
options: It changes original pages and immediately exposes them to every transaction
It changes only log records; data pages are never updated
It changes copies of pages before publishing them at commit
It publishes copied pages before deciding whether to commit
questions.explanation: Copy-on-write keeps changes on copied pages until they can be published. It does not modify the original pages in place and simply hope that no failure occurs.

questions.prompt: What is the intuition behind pessimistic concurrency control?
options: Run first and validate only at commit
Let reads ignore all uncommitted writes
Wait for a crash and use recovery instead of isolation
Prevent harmful conflicts before allowing operations to proceed
questions.explanation: Pessimistic control manages access in advance. This can require waiting, rather than allowing every operation to proceed immediately.

questions.prompt: What expectation motivates optimistic concurrency control?
options: Conflicts are relatively rare and can be checked and handled afterward
Every change can be exposed immediately without validation
No transaction needs to roll back after it starts
All conflicts are prevented before every access
questions.explanation: Optimistic methods typically record activity and validate it, rolling back when necessary. They do not eliminate the possibility of failure.

questions.prompt: A database has CHECK quantity >= 0. A transaction satisfies this check but forgets to credit the receiving warehouse. What follows?
options: This CHECK proves all business-level consistency requirements
Satisfying one constraint does not prove that all business invariants hold
Atomicity automatically supplies the missing addition
Durability automatically preserves the total-stock invariant
questions.explanation: A constraint checks only the condition that was declared. Preserving total inventory is a separate invariant that the transaction must maintain.

questions.prompt: Aborted transactions leave no changes, but committed transactions are lost after a crash. Which assessment is correct?
options: All ACID properties hold because aborts work correctly
Only isolation fails
Atomicity may hold while durability fails
Atomicity and durability are the same property
questions.explanation: Atomicity and durability address different requirements. Correctly handling an abort does not guarantee preservation of committed work.

questions.prompt: What must a valid schedule preserve within each transaction?
options: The arrival order of all transactions
Every COMMIT must occur at the end of the entire system's schedule
The transaction's internal operation order
Transactions must never be interleaved
questions.explanation: A schedule may interleave transactions, but it must preserve each transaction's program order. It need not be serial.

questions.prompt: What is a serial schedule?
options: A schedule that always follows COMMIT order
A schedule that interleaves only reads
A schedule whose BEGIN and COMMIT orders match, even when operations interleave
A schedule that does not interleave operations from different transactions
questions.explanation: A serial schedule runs transactions without interleaving them. It need not follow timestamp order or the order in which transactions arrived.

questions.prompt: Must a serializable schedule be serial?
options: No; it may interleave operations while remaining equivalent to a serial order
Yes; no operations may be interleaved
Yes; BEGIN order must always match the complete execution order
No; every interleaved schedule is serializable
questions.explanation: Serializability is an equivalence property, not a requirement to avoid interleaving. However, not every interleaving is serializable.

questions.prompt: Initially A=30 and B=70. T1 moves 4 from A to B; T2 reads the total after the debit to A but before the credit to B. What total does T2 obtain?
questions.explanation: T2 reads 26 and 70, giving 96 rather than the total of 100 in either serial order. A correct final database state does not repair an incorrect answer already returned.

questions.prompt: T1 and T2 are submitted together. Does serializability promise that the equivalent serial order follows COMMIT order?
options: Yes; COMMIT always determines the serial order
Yes; the shorter transaction always comes first
No; the schedule only needs to match a suitable serial order
No equivalent serial order is required at all
questions.explanation: Serializability does not itself impose start-time or commit-time order. An equivalent serial order must nevertheless exist.

questions.prompt: Which pair of operations conflicts under the lecture's definition?
options: R1(X) and R2(X)
W1(X) and R2(Y), where X differs from Y
R1(X) and W1(X)
R1(X) and W2(X)
questions.explanation: Conflicting operations belong to different transactions, access the same object, and include at least one write. Two reads of X do not conflict.

questions.prompt: T1 reads a price of 8. T2 changes it to 9 and commits; T1 then reads 9. What anomaly occurs?
options: An unrepeatable read
A dirty read of T2's uncommitted value
A lost update caused by one write overwriting another
A dirty write in which T1 overwrites uncommitted data
questions.explanation: T1 reads the same object twice and obtains different values. T2 has committed, so this example is not a dirty read.

questions.prompt: T2 reads a price written by T1 before T1 aborts. What is the immediate problem?
options: An unrepeatable read between two committed values
A dirty read
A lost update caused solely by two transactions writing simultaneously
A dirty write even though T2 has not written anything
questions.explanation: T2 reads an uncommitted value that is later withdrawn. The read is dirty from the moment it occurs, regardless of whether T1 eventually commits or aborts; two read-only operations alone do not cause this anomaly.

questions.prompt: T1 and T2 both read 9 available seats. Each subtracts 1 and writes 8. What result should the business operation produce?
options: 8, because two customers always count as one booking
9, because a write does not change a read
7; a result of 8 has lost one update
10, because concurrency adds a seat
questions.explanation: Two bookings should reduce availability by two. Both transactions use the old value and overwrite one another, so 8 omits one decrement.

questions.prompt: T1 writes X and T2 writes Y, where X differs from Y. Do these two operations alone conflict?
options: Yes, because both are writes
Yes, because belonging to different transactions is sufficient
Yes, if neither transaction has committed
No, because they access different objects
questions.explanation: Different transactions are not sufficient for a conflict: the operations must also access the same object. Writes to independent objects do not conflict in this model.

questions.prompt: What must two conflict-equivalent schedules preserve?
options: The same operations and the order of every conflicting pair
Only the final values in one test database
Only the order of each object's final writes
Only BEGIN and COMMIT order
questions.explanation: Conflict equivalence is a structural condition on operations. Matching final values in one test run is insufficient.

questions.prompt: Which adjacent operations can be swapped without changing conflict order?
options: W1(A) and R2(A)
R1(A) and R2(A)
W1(A) and W2(A)
R1(A) and W2(A)
questions.explanation: Two reads do not conflict. Every other pair accesses A and includes a write, so those operations cannot be freely exchanged.

questions.prompt: Is R1(A), W1(A), R2(B), W2(B) conflict-serializable when A differs from B?
options: No, because it contains two writes
No, because two transactions can be interleaved
Yes; the transactions access independent objects
Only if COMMIT order matches BEGIN order
questions.explanation: No pair of operations conflicts across the two transactions, so either serial order is suitable. This structural conclusion does not depend on particular data values.

questions.prompt: Can R1(A), R2(A), W1(A), W2(A) be conflict-equivalent to a serial schedule?
options: Yes, because every read precedes every write
Yes, because there is only one object
No, because the two reads conflict with one another
No, because R1 before W2 and R2 before W1 impose opposite orders
questions.explanation: R1→W2 requires T1 before T2, while R2→W1 requires T2 before T1. The reads do not conflict with each other; their conflicts with writes create the problem.

questions.prompt: What is proved by turning a schedule into a serial one using only swaps of adjacent nonconflicting operations?
options: The schedule is conflict-serializable
The schedule cannot cause cascading aborts
The schedule is always recoverable, even with dirty reads
The schedule provides strict serializability in real-time order
questions.explanation: These swaps preserve the order of every conflicting pair and therefore prove conflict serializability. They do not establish successful commits or real-time ordering.

questions.prompt: Which edge is created when W1(A) occurs before R2(A)?
options: T2 → T1
T1 → T2
Both directions automatically
No edge, because the read occurs later
questions.explanation: The edge points from the transaction performing the earlier conflicting operation to the one performing the later operation. Its direction is not determined simply by which transaction reads or writes.

questions.prompt: How can a serial order be obtained from an acyclic dependency graph?
options: Sort by BEGIN order regardless of edges
Sort by decreasing number of writes
Use a topological sort
Sort by COMMIT order without checking edges
questions.explanation: A topological order respects every before-and-after constraint in the graph. An arbitrary COMMIT order might violate an edge.

questions.prompt: The graph has T1→T2 and T2→T3, with no reverse edges. Which serial order is valid?
questions.explanation: The two edges require T1 before T2 before T3. A direct T1→T3 edge is unnecessary because the ordering follows transitively.

questions.prompt: The graph has T1→T2, T2→T3, and T3→T1. What is the precise conclusion?
options: The schedule is not conflict-serializable
The schedule is not serial because every graph edge forbids interleaving
The schedule can never be view-serializable
The schedule remains conflict-serializable if each transaction writes only one object
questions.explanation: A cycle rules out conflict serializability. It does not automatically rule out weaker equivalence criteria such as view serializability.

questions.prompt: T3 only reads Z, and no other transaction accesses Z. Can adding T3 create a new conflict cycle?
options: Yes; every new transaction creates edges to existing transactions
No; T3 has no edges connecting it to the other transactions
Yes; reads within the same database always conflict
Yes, if T3 starts before T1 but commits after it
questions.explanation: T3 has no conflicting access pair with another transaction, so it introduces no connecting edges. An earlier BEGIN or later COMMIT does not itself create a conflict edge.

questions.prompt: What must view equivalence preserve?
options: The absolute order of every write, including blind writes
Only final writers, without preserving reads-from relationships
The source of each read and the final writer of each object
Only the set of values read in one sample database
questions.explanation: View equivalence preserves reads-from relationships, reads of initial values, and final writers. Unlike conflict equivalence, it need not preserve the order of every conflicting pair.

questions.prompt: The schedule W1(A), W2(A), W1(A) contains no reads. Which serial order is view-equivalent to it?
options: T1 followed by T2
No serial order can be equivalent
T1 alone, with T2 removed
T2 followed by T1
questions.explanation: T1 is the final writer, and there are no reads to preserve. T2→T1 retains that final writer, whereas T1→T2 changes it.

questions.prompt: Is every conflict-serializable schedule also view-serializable?
options: Yes, in the lecture's model
No; the two classes are disjoint
Only when there are no blind writes
Only when every transaction commits in BEGIN order
questions.explanation: Preserving every conflict order preserves the read relationships and final writers required by view equivalence. The reverse implication does not always hold because of blind writes.

questions.prompt: A read sees A's initial value in S1 but a value written by T2 in S2. Are the schedules view-equivalent?
options: Yes, if the numerical values happen to match in one execution
No, because the source of the read has changed
Yes, because the object name is the same
Yes, if COMMIT order is unchanged
questions.explanation: View equivalence preserves where a read obtains its value, rather than merely requiring equal numbers in one particular database state.

questions.prompt: Why is conflict serializability often easier to check than view serializability?
options: It permits more schedules than view serializability
It understands every business rule
It has an efficient acyclic-graph test
It does not require examining writes
questions.explanation: The graph criterion provides an efficient test. Conflict serializability is the more restrictive class; it does not admit more schedules than view serializability.
